så.explanation: "Så" means "so". To give a result, say: "Det regner, så vi bliver hjemme" (It is raining, so we stay home). To say what comes next, it also means "then": "Først spiser vi, og så går vi" (First we eat, and then we go). Do not mix it up with "så" as the past of "at se" (to see): "Jeg så ham" (I saw him).

så at sige.explanation: "Så at sige" means "so to speak". To say something is not exactly true but very close, put it in the middle of the sentence: "Han bor så at sige på kontoret" (He practically lives at the office).

så længe.explanation: "Så længe" means "as long as". Do not mix it up with "indtil" (until): "Jeg bliver, indtil du kommer" (I stay until you come). When you tell someone to wait a while, "så længe" at the end means "for now": "Vent her så længe" (Wait here for now).

så snart.explanation: "Så snart" means "as soon as". It is built from "så" (as) and "snart" (soon). When you only mean "when", use "når" (when) instead: "Når jeg er færdig, ringer jeg" (When I am finished, I will call).

så vidt.explanation: "Så vidt" means "as far as". To say what you know when you are not completely sure, put it before "jeg ved" (I know): "Så vidt jeg ved, kommer han i morgen" (As far as I know, he is coming tomorrow). To say you only just managed something, it also means "only just": "Jeg nåede så vidt toget" (I only just caught the train).

sådan.explanation: "Sådan" means "like that". To show how to do something, say: "Gør det sådan" (Do it like this). To say "a car like that", put "en" after it: "sådan en bil". To cheer someone on, say "Sådan!" (There you go!).

sådan er det bare.explanation: "Sådan er det bare" means "that's just how it is". Literally, it is "so is it just". To accept something you cannot change, say: "Der er kø her, men sådan er det bare" (There is a line here, but that's just how it is).

related.en: that's just the way it is

sådanne.explanation: "Sådanne" means "such". It is used before more than one thing. To say "such a rule" for one thing, use "sådan en regel" (such a rule).

sågar.explanation: "Sågar" means "even". To add a surprising extra, say: "Sågar min lille bror kan gøre det" (Even my little brother can do it). Do not use it for "even if". For that, use "selv om" (even if): "Jeg går ud, selv om det regner" (I go out even if it rains).

såkaldt.explanation: "Såkaldt" means "so-called". It is built from "så" (so) and "kaldt" (called). To use it before a noun, put it between the article and the noun: "den såkaldte chef" (the so-called boss).

således.explanation: "Således" means "like this". It sounds formal. For everyday talk, use "sådan" (like this) instead: "Gør det sådan" (Do it like this).

sårbar.explanation: "Sårbar" means "vulnerable". It is built from "et sår" (a wound) and "-bar", which works like "-able" in English, as in "brugbar" (usable).

såret.explanation: "Såret" means "wounded". To describe a hurt body, say: "en såret soldat" (a wounded soldier). To describe hurt feelings, say: "såret stolthed" (hurt pride).

såsom.explanation: "Såsom" means "such as". It introduces examples after a general word. In everyday talk, "som" (like) works too: "frugt som æbler" (fruit such as apples).

sæbe.explanation: "Sæbe" means "a soap". To say you want some, say: "noget sæbe" (some soap). For washing dishes, use "opvaskemiddel" (dishwashing liquid) instead: "Jeg bruger opvaskemiddel til tallerkenerne" (I use dishwashing liquid for the plates).

sædvanlig.explanation: "Sædvanlig" means "usual". To say something happened as it always does, use "som sædvanligt" (as usual): "Maden var god som sædvanligt" (The food was good as usual).

særegen.explanation: "Særegen" means "distinctive". It is built from "sær" (odd) and "egen" (own).

særlig.explanation: "Særlig" means "special". To say "not very", use "ikke særlig" (not very): "Det er ikke særlig dyrt" (It is not very expensive).

sød.explanation: "Sød" means "sweet", for taste and for kind or cute people. To say someone did something kind, say: "Det er sødt af dig" (That is sweet of you).

sødmælk.explanation: "Sødmælk" means "whole milk". It is built from "sød" (sweet) and "mælk" (milk), but the milk is not sweet.

sølle.explanation: "Sølle" means "measly". To complain about too little money, put it before the noun: "Jeg fik en sølle krone for det" (I got a measly krone for it).

sølv.explanation: "Sølv" means "silver". To say second place in a competition, use it for the medal: "Hun vandt sølv" (She won silver). To name the color, use "sølvfarvet" (silver-colored): "en sølvfarvet bil" (a silver-colored car).

sølvpapir.explanation: "Sølvpapir" means "aluminum foil". It is built from "sølv" (silver) and "papir" (paper). Despite the name, it is made of aluminum, not silver.

søndag.explanation: "Søndag" means "a Sunday". Danish does not capitalize day names, so write "søndag" in the middle of a sentence. To say this coming Sunday, use "på søndag" (on Sunday). To say every Sunday, use "om søndagen" (on Sundays).

sørgelig.explanation: "Sørgelig" means "sad", for a situation or news, not a feeling inside you. To say that you feel sad, use "ked af det" (sad): "Jeg er ked af det" (I am sad). To call a poor result "pathetic", it also fits: "et sørgeligt resultat" (a pathetic result).
